newsitem.title: MEXICO: Banco de Mexico says no need to tighten money.
newsitem.headline: Banco de Mexico says no need to tighten money.

text.p: Mexico's central bank said on Wednesday it saw no reason to tighten its monetary policy given an increase in the country's monetary base.
Banco de Mexico said in a statement the recent increase in monetary base -- a rough measure of money supply -- "in no way means monetary policy has been relaxed."

The central bank said it had detected no signals from either inflation data, the peso or the money market that the increase in monetary base was leading to pressures that would force a change in its monetary policy. Inflation has continued to fall along with interest rates, while measures of money supply broader than monetary base have also declined recently, it said. Credit from the central bank to the private sector has falln in real terms, too, it added.

"We do not currently see any pressures that indicate a need to adjust our monetary policy," the central bank said. "Under these conditions, the central bank does not see a need to adopt a restrictive policy."

Banco de Mexico said tightening monetary policy now would "create an unnecessary obstacle to the economic recovery, greater difficulties for debtors and banks, and, potentially, boost the real appreciation of the exchange rate...."
It pledged to head off any unexpected inflationary pressures from the rise in monetary base.
Economists in recent days had begun to question the central bank's motives for allowing the monetary base to grow at a faster pace than projected.
Some voiced concern the central bank might be bowing to political pressure to give the economy a lift before July's mid-term elections.
But Banco de Mexico moved to head off the speculation, saying earlier on Wednesday the rise in money was only intended to meet a greater-than-expected demand for money.
In the statement later in the day, the central bank said monetary base grew rapidly because of the following factors:
-- Faster-than-expected economic growth in the first quarter.
-- Lower interest rates had created confidence in the economy and reduced the opportunity cost of holding bills and coins versus investing them.
-- Holy Week holidays were longer than usual this year and holidays in early May created additional money demand.
-- Campaigns by political parties ahead of the elections fueled demand for bills and coins because much of the campaign spending was in cash.
